text: Booked 4 months ahead for a holiday and the host cancelled 6 days before our trip claiming 'property unavailable.' The listing was relisted the next day at 40% higher price. Airbnb's response was a $50 voucher and a 'rebooking credit' that didn't come close to covering the new price gap. Rebooking the same area for the same dates now costs $1,200 more than what I originally locked in. This is not guest protection. This is theater. A confirmed booking should mean something.

Incompetent service. The host entered the property without my consent during my stay. This is a clear violation of Airbnb's core rules. I reported it immediately with photo evidence and a written timeline. After 3 weeks of back-and-forth with support agents who clearly hadn't read my previous messages, I received a 50% refund. Multiple requests to clarify why it was not a full refund went unanswered. The lack of accountability is unacceptable for a platform this size.

Good app but the pricing system is broken. I've used Airbnb for years. Browsing is smooth, the search filters are mostly fine, and the app itself is well designed. My problem is the pricing. You find a listing for $80 a night, go through the whole booking process, and get hit with a cleaning fee, a service fee, sometimes local taxes that nearly double the total. It feels intentionally buried. Just show me the real price upfront. Other platforms manage it.

Cleaning fees are out of control. $215 cleaning fee on a $198 two-night stay? What am I actually paying for. I'm leaving the place clean, taking out the trash, washing my own dishes. If a cleaning fee is more than $50 the host should be required to itemise what they're actually doing for that money. We need transparency or we'll all just go back to hotels.

Stayed in a beautiful apartment in Lisbon for 5 nights. The host was incredibly responsive, the place was spotless, and the location was perfect. This is what Airbnb is supposed to be. I will say — I research carefully now. Superhost only, 100+ reviews, read the most recent ones. With that filtering you can still have great experiences. But it takes work to find.

My booking was cancelled because of a missed payment notification sent to an email I don't actively use. No SMS, no in-app notification, no follow-up. I lost my accommodation in Nice 3 days before my trip and had to pay double for a hotel. Airbnb's notification system for critical actions is broken. Why is email the only channel for a payment failure?

The filters need a complete overhaul. There is no way to filter for things that matter when you're working remotely — verified Wi-Fi speed, actual workspace, natural light. I'm spending hours messaging hosts asking the same questions every booking. Airbnb has the inventory, they just haven't built a product for people who stay more than 3 nights.

Host cancelled 12 hours before check-in. We had flights booked, kids excited, everything. The 'rebooking credit' was 30% of what comparable last-minute places now cost. Airbnb's customer service was polite but the system protects hosts more than guests. Hosts can cancel with limited consequences. Guests can cancel and lose money. The asymmetry is the whole problem.

Mixed feelings. The platform works fine. When you find a good host the experience is great. When something goes wrong support is slow and the resolution is rarely what you hoped for. I had a host who didn't reply to messages for 18 hours before check-in. Airbnb support eventually intervened but I'd been worrying for half a day. The platform needs to enforce host response times or push for hotel-like reliability.

I host a family cabin and the platform has worked well for me over 5 years. Good guests, easy management, the tools have improved. My only real complaint is that the new fee structure squeeze hosts indirectly — guests see cleaning fees and blame us, when most of us are just covering actual cleaning costs. The 'guest pays everything' fee model is creating bad will that hosts wear.

AirCover is a marketing fiction. We had $4,200 in real damages from a party — broken furniture, cigarette burns, missing items. Documented everything with photos, receipts, contractor estimates. Submitted the claim. Six weeks later, 23 message exchanges, six different agents, the final award was $1,950 because they apply depreciation to everything and refuse to cover lost income. 'Up to a million dollars in protection' is the most misleading marketing on the internet.

Used Airbnb for a 2-week stay in Tokyo. The apartment was great. The booking process is overly complex though. I want a 'monthly stay' discount toggle to be more prominent. I want to see total price in the search, not nightly. And the filters could use work — adding a 'remote work friendly' filter would save everyone time. Overall it's still my preferred option for longer trips but with caveats.

Description said 'quiet apartment in central neighbourhood.' Apartment is directly above a bar that operates until 2am. Could not sleep first night. Photos showed an ocean view that was a parking lot. After arrival photos. Airbnb refund process refunded the unused nights but the listing is still live with the same misleading description. Why is this allowed.

As a host, the rating distribution is unfair. A 4-star review tanks our Superhost status. Guests think 4 stars is good. We message guests reminding them what the scale means which feels desperate. Either fix the scale or fix the threshold. The current system rewards politeness in raters and punishes hosts who get honest moderate reviews.

Took my partner to Sedona for our anniversary. The host had been doing this for 10 years and it showed — written instructions, local recommendations, charging cables of every type in a drawer. The trip was perfect. This is the Airbnb that the early reviews talked about. It exists. You just have to filter carefully.

My account was suspended without explanation 4 days before a booking. I could not access my booking, contact my host, or get a response from support for 11 days. The auto-response said 1-3 business days. I missed my check-in. I'm out the booking cost and the cost of last-minute alternative accommodation. The account verification process needs human oversight for legitimate users.

I'm a Superhost with 2 properties. Platform works fine for me. The biggest frustration is the review compression — 4.8 average is the bar and the actual rating distribution is so tight that one mediocre guest can derail a quarter. Otherwise Smart Pricing is okay, the analytics dashboard has improved, support is decent for hosts. Don't trust it for guests though — that's a different story.

Arrived at 10pm after a long flight, lockbox code didn't work, host unresponsive for an hour. Standing outside a building in Madrid with a suitcase, called Airbnb, they put me on hold for 25 minutes. Eventually offered me alternative accommodation 'no guarantee on quality.' Booked a hotel from my phone instead. Refund came 4 days later. This is exactly the failure mode hotels don't have.

Solid platform for vacation rentals. I've used it 50+ times. The product works. Customer support is where it falls down. When everything goes right, great experience. When things go wrong, you're routed through chatbots and script-reading agents who change every message. I'd pay more for a tier with real human support.

Last 3 stays the apartments didn't match the photos. Photos are wide-angle and old. There should be a 'photos taken within last 6 months' verification. The trust in photos has eroded to where I now message every host asking for new photos before booking, which is absurd.

Best platform for long stays. Did 8 weeks in Mexico City for $1,200/month in a beautiful 1BR. You can't do that anywhere else. Find a good host and you can live like a local for less than rent in most cities. The platform isn't perfect but the value proposition is real if you're willing to do the search work.

The 72-hour window for hosts to accept refund requests is absurd. Guests lose right to partial refunds while the host drags out responses. The system favours hosts in disputes and the timing rules are weaponised. Listings also fail to disclose important details — in my case the property was in council housing, complete dealbreaker if disclosed. By the time you arrive and discover, you've lost the money.

Airbnb is fine for what it is. I use it for family trips because we need the space for 4 people. Most stays are okay. The platform fees and cleaning fees make it less of a bargain than it used to be — once you total it up, a hotel suite is often comparable cost with more predictability. The math is closer than the marketing suggests.

Booked a place that turned out to have a non-functioning heating system in November. Apartment was 4 degrees. Host sent me a YouTube video about how the heater works. Stayed two nights in my coat. Airbnb refunded the rest after I moved to a hotel. Why is heating not in basic listing verification.

Total price displayed in search is the single most needed change. I'm comparing 5 listings and have to click through each to see the actual cost. Three of them I'd never have clicked if the total was shown. This is dark pattern design and the company knows it.

Hosting on Airbnb for 7 years. Was a great experience for 5. The last 2 have been a slow decline in support quality and a constant pressure to upgrade everything. After my last damage claim experience — they paid 40% of documented damage with depreciation applied — I'm moving primary listing to Vrbo. Less polished platform but the host experience feels less adversarial. Long-time hosts know.

Used Airbnb in 12 countries. It's the default and there's no real alternative for the inventory breadth. The product works. The two biggest problems are pricing transparency and host cancellations. Both have known solutions. The platform hasn't fixed them which suggests they're not actually prioritised. Still using it because of inventory. Loyalty is paper thin.

Host left dirty dishes in cupboards, hair in the bathroom drain, stained pillowcase. Charged €95 cleaning fee. I had to clean before using the bathroom. Took photos, contacted support, got €45 back. The host was 'apologetic' but the cleaning fee process is reactive. Why am I doing the work of verifying a service I paid for. Make hosts deliver on what they charge for.

Filters are limited and dated. I want to filter for desk, natural light, real workspace, verified Wi-Fi speed. Booking dot com has more useful filters for actual stays. Airbnb is competing on inventory and brand at this point — the product itself hasn't moved much for guests in years. The host tools have improved. The guest tools haven't.

I'm a host who's been at this 3 months. Honest review of the host experience: the onboarding is overwhelming, the pricing benchmarks are vague, the cleaning fee guidance is nonexistent, I'm learning everything by trial and error. Once you figure it out the platform works fine but the new-host experience needs serious thought. There should be a mentorship system or community for first-time hosts. The current docs aren't enough.
